y-m-36-01.title: Counting the real roots of an equation with m in it
y-m-36-01.topic: Number of real roots of an equation with a letter coefficient, and checking assumptions
y-m-36-01.goal: In a solution where every calculation looks correct, find the line that "can only be used on top of some assumption," find every case where there is exactly one real root, and check the range by substituting values.
y-m-36-01.material: Jihu solved the problem below, which asks for the range of m for which the equation mx² − 4x + 1 = 0 in x (m is a real number) has two distinct real roots. The problem says only "equation" and does not say "quadratic equation." A real root is a solution that is a real number, and if the two roots are the same value (a double root), it counts as one real root. (Read as: m times x squared minus 4x plus 1 equals 0)
y-m-36-01.thinking.0: Examine what assumption each line of the solution stands on
y-m-36-01.thinking.1: Find on your own the values where you must split into cases
y-m-36-01.thinking.2: Check the range you found with specific values
y-m-36-01.prereq.0: How to decide the number of roots of a quadratic equation (Grade 10 equations unit level)
y-m-36-01.prereq.1: Telling linear equations and quadratic equations apart — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Jihu's solution that has a problem. Line numbers start from line 1.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put specific values such as 3, 0, and −1 in for m, write out the actual equation, and count the real roots yourself.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare what you counted with the conclusion in line 4. If any value does not match, look at what shape the equation takes at that value.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.line.0: To have two distinct real roots, the discriminant must satisfy D > 0.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the required range is m < 4.
y-m-36-01.s.s1.explain: The calculations in lines 2 and 3 (D = 16 − 4m, m < 4) are correct. The problem is line 1. D > 0 is the condition for two real roots only when the equation is quadratic, but in this problem, if m = 0 the equation becomes the linear equation −4x + 1 = 0, which has just one real root, x = 1/4. So the conclusion in line 4, m < 4, wrongly includes m = 0. Whether you picked line 1 or line 4, you saw the same gap from different places. If you only doubted the first three lines, you were just rechecking the calculation, and the key point of this problem is that the calculation was correct.
y-m-36-01.s.s2.prompt: Find two different values of m for which the equation mx² − 4x + 1 = 0 has exactly one real root, and enter them. (m is a real number)
y-m-36-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a value for m, write out the equation, and first check the form of the expression in x (what degree it is).
y-m-36-01.s.s2.hint.1: There are two different reasons for having one real root. Think about the gap you found in the previous step and the case where the roots coincide.
y-m-36-01.s.s2.ok.c1: For this m, there is exactly one real root.
y-m-36-01.s.s2.fail.c1: For this m, there is not exactly one real root. Put m in, write out the equation yourself, and count the roots.
y-m-36-01.s.s2.explain: If m = 0, then −4x + 1 = 0, so there is only x = 1/4, and if m = 4, then 4x² − 4x + 1 = (2x − 1)² = 0, so x = 1/2 is one root counted twice. These are two cases where there is one real root for different reasons. m = 1 gives two real roots, and m = 5 and m = −3 give 0 and 2 real roots respectively.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.prompt: Which of these is the "range of m for which there are two distinct real roots" from the corrected solution? Whichever m you put in, you can write out the equation yourself and count the roots to check.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.hint.0: Put in m = −1, 1, 0, 4, 5 one at a time and organize the number of real roots in a table.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.hint.1: In the table, look at which interval the values of m with two real roots gather in, and where it breaks off.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.o.a: All real numbers m with m < 4
y-m-36-01.s.s3.r.a: This judgment has not yet checked what shape the equation takes at m = 0.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.r.b: You left out the value where the degree changes and then applied the inequality.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.r.c: Count by hand whether there are two real roots when m is negative too (for example, m = −1). You may have thought m had to be positive for the equation to be quadratic.
y-m-36-01.s.s3.r.d: At m = 4 the two roots coincide, so they are not two distinct real roots. You did not distinguish "has real roots" from "distinct."
y-m-36-01.s.s3.explain: If m = −1, then −x² − 4x + 1 = 0 has two real roots, and if m = 1, then x² − 4x + 1 = 0 also has two real roots. m = 0 gives a linear equation (1 real root) and m = 4 gives a double root (1 real root), so they drop out of the range. Therefore m < 4 and m ≠ 0.

y-m-36-02.title: Does knowing one root fix the coefficients?
y-m-36-02.topic: One root of a quadratic equation and the information needed to determine the coefficients
y-m-36-02.goal: Work out how many coefficients the information "one root is given" fixes, pick out the extra information that is enough to fix the coefficients to one answer, and build an example that satisfies the conditions yourself.
y-m-36-02.material: For the quadratic equation x² + ax + b = 0 (a and b are real numbers), all you know is that x = 2 is a root. Soyeong said, "If you substitute x = 2, you can find a and b," and Daon said, "That alone is not enough information." (Read as: x squared plus a x plus b equals 0)
y-m-36-02.thinking.0: Compare the amount of information (number of equations) with the number of unknowns to find
y-m-36-02.thinking.1: Test one by one whether the extra information is enough
y-m-36-02.thinking.2: Build an example that satisfies all the conditions
y-m-36-02.prereq.0: The meaning of a root of an equation (substituting the root makes the equation true)
y-m-36-02.prereq.1: The relationship between the two roots of a quadratic equation and its coefficients (Grade 10 equations unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.prompt: Compare what Soyeong and Daon said, and choose the most fitting judgment about the information known right now.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a = 0, 1, −1 one at a time, and adjust b so that x = 2 is a root.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether all the pairs you made satisfy the conditions. If so, how many answers are there?
y-m-36-02.s.s1.o.a: The single equation you get by substituting x = 2 lets you find both a and b.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.r.a: This treats one equation as able to fix two unknowns. Try finding what b becomes when a is 0, 1, and −1.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.o.b: If x = 2 is a root, then b must be 0.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.r.b: You did not check whether there is any reason for b to be 0 when the root is not 0. Find b when a = 0.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.o.c: Since only one root is given, this equation must have a double root.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.r.c: This judgment treats "one known root" and "only one root" as the same thing. Find all the roots when a = −1.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.o.d: Substituting gives only one equation, so a and b cannot be fixed to a single answer.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.r.d: This judgment compares the number of unknowns with the number of equations obtained.
y-m-36-02.s.s1.explain: Substituting x = 2 gives one equation, 4 + 2a + b = 0. There are two unknowns, a and b, so infinitely many pairs are possible, such as (a, b) = (0, −4), (−1, −2), (1, −6). Just because one root is given does not mean the other root has the same value.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.prompt: Suppose each is given separately. Choose all the extra information that is enough to fix a and b to a single answer.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, write the new information as an equation and solve it together with the equation you already have, 4 + 2a + b = 0, then count how many pairs (a, b) come out.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.hint.1: For options that do not fix the answer, check by building two different pairs that satisfy the condition.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.r.a: You checked whether knowing both roots fixes both a and b through the sum and product.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.r.b: This judgment checks whether you can find b by combining it with the equation you already have, 4 + 2a + b = 0.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.o.c: a and b are both integers.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.r.c: You did not count how many pairs satisfying 4 + 2a + b = 0 the integer condition leaves. (0, −4) and (−2, 0) are both integer pairs.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.o.d: The two roots are distinct real numbers.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.r.d: You did not distinguish information that narrows the range from information that fixes a single answer. There are also many pairs (a, b) that satisfy this condition.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.r.e: This judgment checks whether the newly given relationship, together with the first equation, makes two equations.
y-m-36-02.s.s2.explain: If the other root is −3, then the sum −1 = −a and the product −6 = b fix them. If a = −1, then b = −2. If b = a + 2, then 4 + 2a + a + 2 = 0 gives a = −2, b = 0. The integer condition and the "distinct real numbers" condition only narrow the range, and several pairs remain.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.prompt: This time, make two different pairs (a, b) where a and b are integers and the two roots of x² + ax + b = 0 are distinct positive real numbers, one of which is 2.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.hint.0: First use 4 + 2a + b = 0 to match b to a, then express in terms of a what the other root is.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.hint.1: Try several values of a so that the other root is positive and is not 2.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make both a and b integers.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.fail.c2: When you put in x = 2, the expression does not become 0.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.ok.c3: The other root is a positive number that is not 2.
y-m-36-02.s.s3.fail.c3: The other root is not positive or is equal to 2, so it does not give "two distinct positive roots."
y-m-36-02.s.s3.explain: For example, (a, b) = (−3, 2) gives x² − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)(x − 2), with roots 1 and 2, and (−5, 6) gives roots 2 and 3. (−4, 4) has only one root, 2 (a double root), and (−1, −2) has the other root −1, so neither fits the conditions. Many pairs satisfy all these conditions, so you can also confirm again that the conditions do not fix a single answer.

y-m-36-03.title: When one root is 1+i, what is the other root?
y-m-36-03.topic: The conditions under which the complex root and conjugate property holds
y-m-36-03.goal: Sort out for yourself, checking your judgment each time the information grows, under which conditions (the kind of coefficients) the conjugate root property is guaranteed.
y-m-36-03.material: One root of the quadratic equation x² + px + q = 0 is said to be 1 + i. (i is the imaginary unit with i² = −1, read as: eye) Each time one more piece of information is given, judge what you can say about "the other root."
y-m-36-03.thinking.0: Sort out how far you can go with only the known information
y-m-36-03.thinking.1: Revise your judgment and confidence according to new information
y-m-36-03.thinking.2: Find the conditions under which a property holds, and counterexamples
y-m-36-03.prereq.0: Complex numbers a + bi and conjugate complex numbers, i² = −1
y-m-36-03.prereq.1: Expressing the sum and product of the two roots of a quadratic equation in terms of its coefficients (Grade 10 equations unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.prompt: Receiving the information one piece at a time, each time choose what you can say about the other root "from only what is known right now."
y-m-36-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write down whether the newly given information is about p and q or about the roots.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.hint.1: Before choosing an answer, calculate the sum and product yourself and check whether those values are real numbers.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.info: What is known: one root is 1 + i. Nothing is said about what kind of numbers p and q are.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: From only what is known right now, can the other root be fixed?
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If you do not know what kind of numbers p and q are, the other root could be anything. The honest judgment at this step is to say it cannot be fixed. If you assumed without saying so that "p and q are real" and answered 1 − i, you will get to check in the next step whether that assumption is actually given as information.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The problem does not say p and q are real numbers, but you may have assumed so. If you used an assumption, it is good to write it down.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There is no information about p and q, so it cannot be fixed.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not assume information that was not given, and held back your judgment.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You may have thought of a rule of flipping every sign. Until you check the sum and product yourself, there is no basis for it.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is a double root, the same as 1 + i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This judgment treats "one root is known" and "the roots coincide" as the same.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.info: New information: p and q are both real numbers. If you write the other root as s + ti (s and t are real numbers), then both the sum of the two roots, (1 + s) + (1 + t)i, and the product, (s + 1) + (s − 1)i, must be real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, what is the other root?
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.after: For the sum to be real, 1 + t = 0, so t = −1, and for the product to be real, s − 1 = 0, so s = 1. Therefore the other root is 1 − i. The earlier judgment that it cannot be fixed was right because the information was lacking, and now it has changed because the information has grown.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You matched only the imaginary part so that the sum is real and did not check the product. Work out whether the product is real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If the two roots are the same, the sum 2 + 2i is not a real number. Check whether the sum is real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The new information gives two equations, the sum and the product, yet you kept holding back your judgment as before.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is the value you get by finding s and t that make both the sum and the product real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.info: We change one piece of information. This time, we drop the statement that p and q are real, and say the other root is 2. Then x² + px + q = (x − (1 + i))(x − 2) = x² − (3 + i)x + (2 + 2i), so p = −3 − i and q = 2 + 2i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.after: In this example, p = −3 − i and q = 2 + 2i are not real numbers, so it is a case outside the assumption that "the coefficients are real." Without that assumption, you cannot say that the one root 1 + i alone makes the other root 1 − i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Without the assumption that p and q are real, you cannot say the other root is 1 − i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You distinguished what assumption the conjugate root property stands on.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: If one root is 1 + i, the other root is always 1 − i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Look again at what the other root is in the example we just made.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The roots of a quadratic equation are always one real number and one imaginary number.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The two roots 1 + i and 2 in this example may look like such a pair, but the type of the roots depends on the coefficients. Think of the case where both roots are real when the coefficients are real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Even if p and q are real, the other root may not be 1 − i.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The p and q in this example are not real. Check under what conditions the example was made.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.info: Last piece of information: again p and q are real, but this time one root is 1 + √2, which is not imaginary. For example, if the other root is 3, then (x − (1 + √2))(x − 3) = x² − (4 + √2)x + 3 + 3√2, and here p = −4 − √2 and q = 3 + 3√2 are both real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: Can you say the other root is 1 − √2?
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.after: The condition that p and q are real alone does not fix the other root as 1 − √2. 1 − √2 is guaranteed only when there is the stronger condition that p and q are rational.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.o.a: If p and q are real, it is always 1 − √2.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: Look at what the other root is in the example we just gave.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.o.b: It must be a double root, the same as 1 + √2.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This judgment treats "one root is known" and "a double root" as the same.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You carried over the rule used for imaginary roots, changing only the sign. Check the sum and product.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.o.d: It cannot be fixed. Even if the other root is 3, p and q are real.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: You confirmed with an example that the condition of real coefficients alone is not enough.
y-m-36-03.s.s1.reflect: At first there was no information, so "cannot be fixed" was the right judgment, and when the information "p and q are real" arrived, the judgment changed to 1 − i. In the next two steps, you checked with examples under what conditions the same rule breaks down. Look back at which information arrived and which judgment changed, or whether it was fine to keep it as it was.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the cases where "the other root is necessarily fixed as the conjugate (the form with only the sign changed)."
y-m-36-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, freely pick one other root, and check whether p and q then satisfy the option's condition.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.hint.1: An option for which even one counterexample satisfying the condition can be built is not "necessarily."
y-m-36-03.s.s2.o.a: One root of a quadratic equation whose coefficients are all real is 3 − 2i
y-m-36-03.s.s2.r.a: You checked that both conditions are present: an imaginary root is given and the coefficients are real.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.o.b: One root of a quadratic equation whose coefficients are complex numbers is 3 − 2i
y-m-36-03.s.s2.r.b: Recall the counterexample from the earlier step, and think about whether this rule is guaranteed when there is no assumption that the coefficients are real.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.o.c: One root of a quadratic equation whose coefficients are all rational is 2 + √3
y-m-36-03.s.s2.r.c: This judgment distinguishes what condition on the coefficients is needed for the rule to hold for real roots too.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.o.d: One root of a quadratic equation whose coefficients are all real is 2 + √3
y-m-36-03.s.s2.r.d: This judgment treats the conditions needed for imaginary roots and irrational roots as the same. Think of the example where the other root is 3.
y-m-36-03.s.s2.explain: An imaginary root of a quadratic equation with real coefficients appears together with its conjugate, and the root 2 + √3 of a quadratic equation with rational coefficients appears together with 2 − √3. When the coefficients are complex, or are merely real, an irrational root does not let you fix the other root as its conjugate.

y-m-36-04.title: Lines through the point (0, 4) and the point (0, −4)
y-m-36-04.topic: Number of intersection points of a parabola and a line (simultaneous quadratic equations)
y-m-36-04.goal: Check the first judgment, "changing the slope does not change the number of intersection points," against where the line passes through, and explain why the result differs in the same structure.
y-m-36-04.material: The parabola y = x² is on the coordinate plane. Its vertex is the origin and it opens upward. The point (0, 4) is inside the parabola (above the curve), and the point (0, −4) is outside it (below the curve). m is a real number, and we do not consider lines parallel to the y-axis. The line y = mx + 4 passes through the point (0, 4), and the line y = mx − 4 passes through the point (0, −4). The number of intersection points is the number of real solutions (x, y) of the simultaneous equations.
y-m-36-04.thinking.0: Test the first judgment with specific values
y-m-36-04.thinking.1: Compare how the conclusion changes when the condition (the point it passes through) changes
y-m-36-04.thinking.2: Explain the number of intersection points using the equations and the positions of the figures
y-m-36-04.prereq.0: How to decide the number of roots of a quadratic equation (Grade 10 equations unit level)
y-m-36-04.prereq.1: Reading the line y = mx + n as a line on the coordinate plane — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.prompt: As you change m in the line y = mx + 4 that passes through the point (0, 4), what happens to the number of intersection points with the parabola y = x²? Choose your first judgment.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put in m = 0, 1, 10, −3 one at a time, set x² equal to the line's expression, and count the real roots.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.hint.1: Observe what shape the final equation has, whatever m is.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.o.a: Whatever value m has, there are always 2 intersection points.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment connects the position of the point to the number of intersection points.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.o.b: Depending on the value of m, 0, 1, and 2 intersection points all occur.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.r.b: This judgment assumes a tilted line can miss the parabola. Put in m = 0, 1, 10 and find the intersection points.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.o.c: If m = 0 there is 1 intersection point, and if m ≠ 0 there are 2.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment assumes the horizontal line y = 4 meets the parabola at only one point. Count the solutions of x² = 4.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.o.d: Whatever value m has, there is always 1 intersection point.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.r.d: You may have confused a tangent line with a secant line. Find the intersection points yourself when m = 0.
y-m-36-04.s.s1.explain: x² = mx + 4 becomes x² − mx − 4 = 0, and the value that decides the number of roots is m² + 16, which is greater than 0 whatever m is. So there are always two distinct real roots, that is, 2 intersection points. This is because the point (0, 4) is inside the parabola, so a line in any direction crosses the curve twice.
y-m-36-04.s.s2.prompt: This time it is the line y = mx − 4, which passes through the point (0, −4). Test whether your first judgment ("always the same number") also holds for this line. Enter two different integers m for which this line does not meet the parabola y = x².
y-m-36-04.s.s2.hint.0: When m = 0, draw it or use the equations to check whether y = −4 and y = x² meet.
y-m-36-04.s.s2.hint.1: Changing the value of m, organize in a table whether x² − mx + 4 = 0 has roots or not.
y-m-36-04.s.s2.ok.c2: For this m, the line and the parabola do not meet.
y-m-36-04.s.s2.fail.c2: For this m, the line and the parabola meet. Find the real roots of x² = mx − 4 yourself.
y-m-36-04.s.s2.explain: x² = mx − 4 becomes x² − mx + 4 = 0, and the value that decides the number of roots is m² − 16. If −4 < m < 4 it is negative, so they do not meet; if m = ±4 it is 0, so they meet at one point (a tangent line); and if |m| > 4 they meet at two points. The first judgment held only for the point (0, 4).
y-m-36-04.s.s3.prompt: If you first thought that "changing the slope gives the same number of intersection points," how should you fix that judgment? Compare the two lines (the one through the point (0, 4) and the one through the point (0, −4)) and explain, using the equations or the positions of the points, why the results differ.
y-m-36-04.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the two cases and write x² = mx ± 4 rearranged so that x² and the linear term are on one side.
y-m-36-04.s.s3.hint.1: In the two rearranged equations, compare the part that does not change whatever m is with the part that changes with m.
y-m-36-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: In the case through the point (0, 4), ... , and in the case through the point (0, −4), ...
y-m-36-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In my explanation, is the difference clear that y = mx + 4 always gives 2 while y = mx − 4 changes with m?
y-m-36-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain the reason for the difference using either the equations (m² + 16 and m² − 16) or the position of the points (inside and outside)?
y-m-36-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I rewrite the first judgment, adding a condition saying in which case it is correct?
y-m-36-04.s.s3.model.0: The point (0, 4) is inside the parabola, so y = mx + 4 gives x² − mx − 4 = 0, and since m² + 16 is always positive, there are 2 intersection points for any m. The point (0, −4) is outside, so x² − mx + 4 = 0 gives m² − 16, which makes the number 0, 1, or 2 depending on m. So the first judgment is correct only for lines through the inside point.
y-m-36-04.s.s3.model.1: The idea that it is always the same must be fixed. The line y = mx − 4 does not meet the parabola for −4 < m < 4, meets it at one point for m = ±4, and meets it at two points otherwise. In contrast, a line through (0, 4) meets it at two points for any m. It depends on whether the point the line passes through is inside or outside the parabola.
y-m-36-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: Explained using the position of the points and used the equations only in part.

y-m-36-05.title: The range of k that works for all real numbers x
y-m-36-05.topic: The condition for a quadratic inequality to hold for all real numbers, and the boundary value
y-m-36-05.goal: Tell apart whether the result of checking a few values is evidence or proof, and confirm that whether the boundary value is included changes depending on whether the inequality sign is > or ≥.
y-m-36-05.material: Decide step by step the range of k for which the inequality x² − 4x + k > 0 holds for all real numbers x. (Read as: x squared minus 4x plus k is greater than 0) One more piece of information is given each time.
y-m-36-05.thinking.0: Judge whether the result of checking a few values can be generalized
y-m-36-05.thinking.1: Put in the boundary value yourself to decide whether it is included
y-m-36-05.thinking.2: Compare how the conclusion changes when the condition changes
y-m-36-05.prereq.0: The minimum value and vertex of a quadratic function
y-m-36-05.prereq.1: The relationship between a quadratic inequality and the graph of a quadratic function (Grade 10 equations and inequalities unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is given, choose "what you can say from what is known now."
y-m-36-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put the boundary value of k directly into the expression, rewrite it in the form (x − 2)², and check its value at x = 2.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.hint.1: Put the same value of k into the > case and the ≥ case and compare whether each holds.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.info: With k = 5, putting in x = −1, 0, 2, 3, 6 gave the values of the expression 10, 5, 1, 2, 17 in order, all positive.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say about k = 5?
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Five values are good evidence, but they are not a check of all real numbers. If you know the shape of the expression (the smallest value of this expression), you can be sure, and this expression has its smallest value, 1, at x = 2, so k = 5 does in fact work.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Since all five values are positive, we can be sure it holds for all real numbers x.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment has not yet taken into account the gap between the 5 points checked and all real numbers.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is likely to hold, but the five values alone cannot make us sure.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment distinguishes between the values checked and the generalization.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The value is small at x = 2, so it does not hold.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment says it does not hold because the value is small, even though the value 1 is positive. What the inequality requires is that the value be greater than 0.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Putting in more values will not tell us, so we cannot decide.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You did not tell apart the limit of putting in more values from the fact that the shape of the expression lets you check.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Observation: putting in x = 2 gives the value of the expression 4 − 8 + k = k − 4. And the value at x = 2 is the smallest value of this expression.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then what range can you expect for k?
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.after: The sign of the smallest value k − 4 decides the condition. If k > 4, all the values are positive, and if k < 4, it becomes negative at x = 2. For the boundary k = 4, you have to test it directly to know whether it is included.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is the expectation that the smallest value k − 4 must be greater than 0.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is the expectation that the smallest value k − 4 must be 0 or greater. Before testing the boundary k = 4, this is a reasonable expectation.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You may have mistaken the k = 5 checked earlier for the boundary. Put in k = 4.5.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is the expectation that the expression is always positive when k is positive. Find the value at x = 2 when k = 1.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Boundary test: if k = 4, the expression is x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)². The value at x = 2 is 0, and it is positive at all other x.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: In the original inequality x² − 4x + k > 0, is k = 4 in the range?
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The value at x = 2 is 0, so "greater than 0" does not hold. So k = 4 is left out and the range is k > 4. If you expected b in the previous step, this test changed your expectation, and if you expected a, it confirmed that your expectation was right.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is in. This is because it is positive at most x.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read "all real numbers" as "almost all real numbers."
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: You cannot know whether it is in without seeing the problem.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You could have decided by putting in the boundary value directly, but you did not.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is not in. The value is 0 at x = 2, so > 0 fails.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You judged that if the inequality fails at one point, it does not hold for all real numbers.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.info: Condition change: now change the inequality sign and think about the k for which x² − 4x + k ≥ 0 holds for all real numbers x.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.after: (x − 2)² ≥ 0 holds for all real numbers x, so k = 4 is in and the range is k ≥ 4. Even for the same expression, whether the boundary value is included depends on whether the sign is > or ≥.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.o.a: It is in. Even if the value at x = 2 is 0, ≥ 0 holds.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You judged according to the condition whether 0 is allowed at the boundary.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.o.b: It is not in. It was left out before, so it is left out for the same reason.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You did not take into account that the inequality sign is different from the previous inequality.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.o.c: We cannot tell whether it is in. For a quadratic inequality, you must always solve it anew when the sign changes.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You could have decided by substituting k = 4 directly, but you did not.
y-m-36-05.s.s1.reflect: At first it was reasonable not to be sure from a few values, then putting in the boundary value directly confirmed whether it is included, and when the inequality sign changed, the judgment for the same boundary value changed. Tell which pieces of information changed your judgment and which let your judgment stay as it was.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.prompt: Let us apply this judgment to a new problem. Which of these is the range of k for which the inequality −x² + 6x + k < 0 holds for all real numbers x?
y-m-36-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put in x = 3 and express the value of the expression in terms of k. Think about whether this value is the highest point on the graph.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put in k = −9 and k = −10 directly and compare whether the inequality holds at x = 3.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.r.a: After rewriting the expression, check whether the signs and constant calculations are right by using the largest value of −x² + 6x.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.r.b: You found the largest value of −x² + 6x + k and judged that it must be less than 0.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.r.c: You did not check whether at the boundary k = −9 the largest value becomes 0, so that < 0 fails.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.r.d: You read the direction of the inequality sign the other way. Find the value at x = 3 when k = 0.
y-m-36-05.s.s2.explain: −x² + 6x + k = −(x − 3)² + 9 + k, so the largest value is 9 + k at x = 3. This value must be less than 0, so k < −9, and if k = −9 the value at x = 3 is 0, so < 0 fails.

y-m-36-06.title: Finding k so that there are seven integer solutions
y-m-36-06.topic: Solutions of an absolute value inequality and the number of integer solutions
y-m-36-06.goal: Read the solution of an absolute value inequality as an interval, work out how the number of integer solutions changes with the parameter, make several values that satisfy the condition, and explain their range.
y-m-36-06.material: For a positive number k, count the integers x that satisfy the inequality |x − 1| ≤ k. (Read as: the absolute value of x minus 1 is less than or equal to k) For example, if k = 1.5, the integers x are 0, 1, 2, so there are 3.
y-m-36-06.thinking.0: Find the points where the count changes as the parameter changes
y-m-36-06.thinking.1: Make several values that satisfy the condition
y-m-36-06.thinking.2: Explain the range by working out whether the boundary value is included
y-m-36-06.prereq.0: Writing the solution of the absolute value inequality |x − a| ≤ b as an interval
y-m-36-06.prereq.1: Counting integers on the number line (Grade 10 equations and inequalities unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.prompt: If you start k at 2 and increase it little by little, when does the number of integers x change?
y-m-36-06.s.s1.hint.0: For k = 2, 2.5, 2.9, 3, write the solution as an interval and list the integers in it one by one.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.hint.1: Mark what value the end of the interval has when a new integer comes in.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.o.a: It changes every time k grows by 0.1.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.r.a: You did not count the integer solutions yourself when k is 2.1 or 2.5. Write down what interval the solution is.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.o.b: It changes every time k grows by 2.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.r.b: You did not check whether the count already differs at k = 3. Compare the solutions for k = 2 and k = 3.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.o.c: It does not change even when k grows.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.r.c: You did not write the solution intervals for k = 2 and k = 4 and compare by counting the integers.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.o.d: It changes every time k becomes an integer.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.r.d: You connected the times when both ends of the solution interval are integers with the times when the count changes.
y-m-36-06.s.s1.explain: The solution is 1 − k ≤ x ≤ 1 + k. If k = 2, then −1 ≤ x ≤ 3, which has 5 integers, and even if k is 2.1, 2.5, or 2.9, the same integers −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 are in, as in −1.9 ≤ x ≤ 3.9. When k = 3, both ends −2 and 4 are integers, so two are added at once.
y-m-36-06.s.s2.prompt: Enter two or more different values of k for which there are exactly 7 integers x. (k is positive and may be a decimal)
y-m-36-06.s.s2.hint.0: For 7 integers in a row, first decide what the middle integer would be.
y-m-36-06.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a k, write the interval 1 − k ≤ x ≤ 1 + k, and count the integers in it yourself to check.
y-m-36-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of integers x is not 7. Count the integers in 1−k ≤ x ≤ 1+k yourself.
y-m-36-06.s.s2.explain: If k = 3, then −2 ≤ x ≤ 4, with 7 integers −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and if k = 3.5, then −2.5 ≤ x ≤ 4.5, with the same 7. If k = 4, then −3 and 5 are added, making 9, and if k = 2.9, then −1.9 ≤ x ≤ 3.9, which has 5.
y-m-36-06.s.s3.prompt: Based on the values you just made, write the range of k for which there are exactly 7 integers x as an inequality, and explain why inclusion differs at the two ends of that range.
y-m-36-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the two ends of the interval for k = 3 and for k = 4, and compare whether any new integer comes in.
y-m-36-06.s.s3.hint.1: Also check whether the number of integers changes when you put in values between 3 and 4 (for example, 3.2, 3.8).
y-m-36-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: For there to be 7 integer solutions, k is ... because ...
y-m-36-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the range I wrote, did I check by counting the integers myself that k = 3 is included and k = 4 is not?
y-m-36-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain why inclusion differs at the two ends by connecting it to "how many integers come in"?
y-m-36-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I write it knowing that values that are not integers, like k = 3.9, are also in the range?
y-m-36-06.s.s3.model.0: For the integer solutions to be the 7 integers from −2 to 4, 3 ≤ k < 4. At k = 3 the ends of the interval are exactly −2 and 4, so there are 7, but when k = 4, −3 and 5 also come in, making 9, so 4 is not included.
y-m-36-06.s.s3.model.1: If k is at least 3 and less than 4, there are 7. If it is 3, the interval is −2 ≤ x ≤ 4, and even at 3.9 no new integer comes in. The moment it becomes 4, −3 and 5 are added and the count changes, so 4 must be left out.

y-m-36-07.title: What range of a gives a common part?
y-m-36-07.topic: The condition for a system of linear inequalities to have a solution (the boundary value)
y-m-36-07.goal: When deciding the condition for two inequalities to have a common part, confirm by direct substitution that the result at the boundary value differs depending on the kind of inequality sign, and suggest a way to disprove a wrong judgment.
y-m-36-07.material: Minsu found the range of a for which the system of inequalities 3x − 1 > 5 , x − a ≤ 3 (x is a real number, a is a real constant) has a solution, as follows. "Has a solution" means there is at least one x that satisfies both inequalities. (Read as: 3x minus 1 is greater than 5, x minus a is less than or equal to 3)
y-m-36-07.thinking.0: Check whether the handling of the boundary in the solution is correct
y-m-36-07.thinking.1: Compare the results at the boundary value depending on the kind of inequality sign
y-m-36-07.thinking.2: Suggest a way to verify a judgment by substituting values
y-m-36-07.prereq.0: Writing the solution of a linear inequality as an interval on the number line
y-m-36-07.prereq.1: The solution of a system of inequalities is the common part of the solutions of each inequality — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-07.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one wrong line in Minsu's solution. Line numbers start from line 1.
y-m-36-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put a = −1 in and rewrite the two inequalities. Mark on a number line whether there is an x that satisfies both conditions.
y-m-36-07.s.s1.hint.1: Mark whether each endpoint of the two intervals from lines 1 and 2 is included in its interval.
y-m-36-07.s.s1.line.2: For there to be a common part, a + 3 ≥ 2 must hold.
y-m-36-07.s.s1.explain: The rearrangements in lines 1 and 2 are correct (x > 2, x ≤ a + 3). The wrong place is line 3. In x > 2, 2 is not included, so if a + 3 = 2, there is no x that satisfies both x > 2 and x ≤ 2. So a + 3 > 2 must hold, and the conclusion in line 4 should be a > −1. If you picked line 4, you pointed at the result that carried on the error in line 3.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.prompt: When c is a real constant, choose all the systems of inequalities that have a solution if c = 3.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, put in c = 3, write the two intervals, and check whether x = 3 is in both intervals.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.hint.1: Draw the two intervals on a number line and compare whether there is a point where they overlap.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.r.a: You checked whether there is a common part when the ends of the two intervals are the same and neither includes the endpoint.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.r.b: You checked the case where both sides include the endpoint, so one point is left.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.r.c: You checked whether there is a common point left when only one side includes the endpoint.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.r.d: You checked whether there is a common part in the opposite case where only one side includes the endpoint.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.r.e: You checked whether the two intervals overlap at one point when the boundaries are the same value.
y-m-36-07.s.s2.explain: When c = 3, option b is x ≥ 3 and x ≤ 3, so x = 3 is a solution. Option e is also x ≤ 3 and x ≥ 3, so x = 3 is a solution. In the others, at least one side does not include the endpoint 3, so there is no common part.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.prompt: What would you tell Minsu? Suggest one way to check for yourself whether Minsu's conclusion a ≥ −1 is right, and write the correct range.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put a = −1 into the two inequalities and rewrite each as an inequality in x.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.hint.1: Mark on a number line whether there is an x where the two inequalities overlap.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Minsu, if you put in a = ... , then ...
y-m-36-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the check I suggested concrete enough for Minsu to try himself?
y-m-36-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I give as my evidence that at a = −1 there is no x for which the two conditions hold at the same time?
y-m-36-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I check by putting in one value that there really is a solution when a > −1?
y-m-36-07.s.s3.model.0: Let's put in a = −1 ourselves. Then x > 2 and x ≤ 2, so there is no x that satisfies both conditions. So a = −1 does not work, and it must be a > −1.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.model.1: If you check by substituting the boundary value −1, the first inequality says x is greater than 2 and the second says x is at most 2, so there is no common part. For there to be a solution, a must be greater than −1. For example, if a = 0, then 2 < x ≤ 3, so there is a solution.
y-m-36-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: Additionally checked by putting in one correct value.

y-m-36-08.title: Which of the two solutions will keep being useful?
y-m-36-08.topic: Integer roots of a cubic equation and comparing solution methods
y-m-36-08.goal: Compare two solution methods, evaluate under what conditions each can be used, and make a plan for solving by building a cubic equation with integer roots yourself.
y-m-36-08.material: Hajun and Seoyun solved the cubic equation x³ − 2x² − x + 2 = 0. Hajun: grouped the first two terms and the last two terms and changed it to x²(x − 2) − (x − 2) = (x − 2)(x² − 1). Seoyun: put in x = 1, confirmed it gives 0, and divided by x − 1 to get (x − 1)(x² − x − 2). Both of them got the roots −1, 1, 2. (Read as: x cubed minus 2x squared minus x plus 2 equals 0)
y-m-36-08.thinking.0: Compare and evaluate the solution methods against each other
y-m-36-08.thinking.1: Judge whether a method can keep being used when the conditions change
y-m-36-08.thinking.2: Build an equation that satisfies the conditions
y-m-36-08.prereq.0: The factor theorem and synthetic division (dividing a polynomial by a linear expression)
y-m-36-08.prereq.1: The fact that candidates for integer roots of an equation with integer coefficients are divisors of the constant term (Grade 10 equations unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most fitting evaluation that compares the two solutions?
y-m-36-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the two solutions, write one line on what feature of the problem (the form of the expression, the constant term) it used.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether each solution could keep being used if one of the two features disappeared.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.o.a: Only Hajun's solution is correct. Seoyun just happened to have x = 1 as a root.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.r.a: This judgment treats finding roots by substitution as not trustworthy.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.o.b: Only Seoyun's solution is correct. Grouping is a trick that works only for this problem.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the range where one method applies and ruled out the other.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.o.c: Both are valid, and the clues each used are different.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.r.c: You distinguished that the two methods use different clues.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.o.d: The answers are the same, so there is no point in evaluating the methods separately.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.r.d: You did not tell apart the fact that the answers are the same from how general a method is.
y-m-36-08.s.s1.explain: Hajun used the structure in which the expression can be organized by grouping, and Seoyun used the divisors of the constant term as candidates to find a root. Both are correct calculations, and the conditions they use are different. This problem satisfied both conditions, so both worked.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.prompt: Change the constant term so the equation is x³ − 2x² − x + 3 = 0. Which is the correct statement about this expression?
y-m-36-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put in x = 1, −1, 3, −3 and calculate the value of the expression for each.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how the signs of the value of the expression differ at x = −2 and x = −1.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.o.a: Hajun's grouping works as it is, and the factoring is finished right away.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.r.a: You did not actually write out whether a common factor really remains after grouping. Check that the last two terms are −x + 3.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.o.b: Putting in ±1, ±3 gives values that are all not 0, so there is no integer root.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.r.b: You distinguished how far the method of trying all the integer candidates can tell you.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.o.c: There is no integer root, so this equation has no solution and the solving is over.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.r.c: You treated "no integer root" and "no solution" as the same. Compare the signs of the value of the expression at x = −2 and x = −1.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.o.d: Neither grouping nor substitution works, so this equation cannot be solved.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.r.d: This judgment says that if the methods within the integers get stuck, there is no other method. Think about how you can know a real root exists.
y-m-36-08.s.s2.explain: Putting in x = 1, −1, 3, −3 gives the values of the expression 1, 1, 9, −39, none of which is 0, so there is no integer root. But at x = −2 it is −11 and at x = −1 it is 1, so there is a real root between them. It is not that there is no solution; it just does not land on an integer.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.prompt: This time, for x³ − 2x² − x + c = 0, make (r, c) so that the integer r is a root. Enter three examples with different values of c. (r and c are both integers)
y-m-36-08.s.s3.hint.0: Put an integer in for r and solve the equation r³ − 2r² − r + c = 0 for c.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.hint.1: Try several r and organize in a table whether there are cases where c is the same.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make r and c integers.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.ok.c2: r is a root of this equation.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.fail.c2: When you put in r, the expression does not become 0. Put r into the expression and adjust c.
y-m-36-08.s.s3.explain: If r is a root, then from r³ − 2r² − r + c = 0, c is fixed as c = −r³ + 2r² + r. r = 1, 2, −1 all give c = 2, so they are the same equation, and r = 0 gives c = 0, r = 3 gives c = −6, and r = −2 gives c = 14. The condition of finding examples with different c keeps you from counting the same equation with a different root.
y-m-36-08.s.s4.prompt: Briefly write a plan for solving a cubic equation that you can use whatever integer the constant term is. Include what you would do when grouping does not work and when all the integer candidates fail.
y-m-36-08.s.s4.hint.0: Number which of grouping, substitution, and dividing you will try, and in what order.
y-m-36-08.s.s4.hint.1: Work out what you can know and what you cannot know when none of the values you substituted gives 0.

If none of the candidates works, it means there is no integer root, so think of another method to see where the real roots are.

y-m-36-09.title: A quadratic equation whose sum and product are both positive
y-m-36-09.topic: The signs of the two roots of a quadratic equation and conditions on the sum and product
y-m-36-09.goal: Find the missing condition in the claim "if the sum and product are both positive, both roots are positive" by building a counterexample yourself, and fix the claim so it becomes true.
y-m-36-09.material: Mina made a claim: "For the quadratic equation x² − sx + q = 0 (s and q are real numbers), if the sum s and the product q of the two roots are both positive, then both roots are positive real numbers." (Read as: x squared minus s x plus q equals 0) The sum of the two roots is s and the product is q.
y-m-36-09.thinking.0: Judge whether the claim always holds
y-m-36-09.thinking.1: Build a counterexample that satisfies the condition but breaks the conclusion
y-m-36-09.thinking.2: Fix the claim by adding a condition under which it holds
y-m-36-09.prereq.0: The relationship that expresses the sum and product of the two roots of a quadratic equation in terms of its coefficients
y-m-36-09.prereq.1: How to judge whether the roots of a quadratic equation are real or not (Grade 10 equations unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose your first judgment about Mina's claim.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a few pairs of specific positive numbers for s and q and find the roots of the equation yourself.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether there are cases where the roots are not real, and work out whether the conclusion "positive real numbers" is still right then.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.o.a: It holds only when the sum is positive and the product is negative.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.r.a: You read backwards the relationship that if the product is positive, the two roots have the same sign.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.o.b: There are cases where it does not hold. One root may be negative.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.r.b: You missed that if the product is positive, two real roots have the same sign. For example, build a few pairs of two real roots whose sum is positive and product is positive.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.o.c: It always holds. If the sum and product are positive, both roots are positive.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.r.c: You did not test counterexamples to see whether the signs of the sum and product alone are enough.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.o.d: It may not hold. There are cases where the roots are not real.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.r.d: You checked the assumption that the roots must be real for the signs of the sum and product to tell us the signs of the roots.
y-m-36-09.s.s1.explain: If the product is positive and both roots are real, the two roots have the same sign, and if the sum is positive, both are positive. But if the roots are not real, that is, imaginary roots, the word "sign" cannot be used, and the sum and product can still be positive. For example, the roots of x² − 2x + 5 = 0 are 1 ± 2i.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.prompt: Make two different pairs (s, q) that break Mina's claim. The sum s and the product q are both positive, but the two roots of the equation x² − sx + q = 0 must not be positive real numbers.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a value for s, then make q gradually larger and observe how the roots of the equation change.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.hint.1: For each s, find about where the boundary of q lies that separates real roots from non-real roots.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The sum and product are both positive.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.fail.c1: s and q must both be greater than 0.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The two roots are not real, so the claim breaks.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.fail.c2: For this (s, q), the two roots are real. Solve the equation and check whether the roots are real.
y-m-36-09.s.s2.explain: If (s, q) = (2, 5), the roots are 1 ± 2i; if (1, 1), the roots are (1 ± √3 i)/2; if (4, 10), the roots are 2 ± √6 i. (5, 6) has the positive real roots 2 and 3, and (4, 4) has just one root, 2 (a double root), which is a positive real number, so neither breaks the claim. The counterexamples are the cases where the roots are imaginary even though the sum and product are positive.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.prompt: What condition must you add for Mina's claim to become a correct claim? Write the reason too, mentioning the counterexample you just made.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.hint.0: For the (s, q) you made as a counterexample, find the roots of the equation yourself and check whether they are real.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.hint.1: Write what condition could filter out that counterexample while leaving the conditions on the sum and product as they are.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The condition that the two roots ... is also needed. This is because ...
y-m-36-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I check that the condition I added blocks the counterexample (are the counterexample's roots real)?
y-m-36-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I write knowing why the sign conditions on the sum and product are still needed (the signs are the same, and the sum is positive)?
y-m-36-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I check with one value that Mina's claim is true even with the condition I added?
y-m-36-09.s.s3.model.0: You must add the condition that the two roots are real, that is, the discriminant condition s² − 4q ≥ 0. Then, since the product is positive, the two roots have the same sign, and since the sum is positive, both are positive. The counterexample s = 2, q = 5 has a negative discriminant, so the roots are imaginary and it gets filtered out.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.model.1: The two roots must be real (D ≥ 0). If you attach this condition to s > 0, q > 0, the claim that both roots are positive real numbers is true. The (1, 1) I made has imaginary roots, so it does not satisfy this condition.
y-m-36-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: Expressed it as the condition of being real without using the word discriminant.

y-m-36-10.title: Possible dimensions of a garden against a wall
y-m-36-10.topic: Designing dimension conditions using a quadratic inequality
y-m-36-10.goal: Write a situation with a length limit as a quadratic inequality, find the range of possible dimensions, and judge how the range changes when a limit is added and in which case there is only one possible dimension.
y-m-36-10.material: A fence rope of exactly 20 m is used to enclose three sides of a rectangular garden. The remaining side is placed against a wall. Let the length of the side against the wall be w m and the length of one side perpendicular to it be x m. Then the rope gives w + 2x = 20. The area is x·w ㎡, and the goal is a garden with an area of at least 48 ㎡. All lengths are greater than 0, and the unit is m.
y-m-36-10.thinking.0: Translate conditions given in sentences into equations and inequalities
y-m-36-10.thinking.1: Judge how the possible range shrinks when a new limit appears
y-m-36-10.thinking.2: Make several designs that satisfy all the conditions
y-m-36-10.prereq.0: Writing the solution of a quadratic inequality as an interval
y-m-36-10.prereq.1: Expressing conditions given in sentences as equations (Grade 10 equations and inequalities unit level) — H2 of this task is only the difficulty and support level in this production allocation; it does not mean the curriculum assigns that subject to that grade. Assume the prerequisite knowledge below has already been learned.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.prompt: Suppose the wall is long enough that there is no limit on the length w. Which is the range of x for which the area is at least 48 ㎡? (x is a real number)
y-m-36-10.s.s1.hint.0: Express w in terms of x and write the area as an expression in x alone, then put in x = 3, 4, 5, 7, calculate the area, and make a table.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, find the interval of x where the area is 48 or more.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.r.a: You wrote the area as an expression in x and read the solution of the inequality as an interval.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.r.b: This judgment says the area keeps growing as x grows. Find w and the area when x = 9.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.r.c: This judgment says the smaller x is, the better. Find the area when x = 1.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.r.d: The problem does not say x must be an integer, but you thought only about integers. Find the area when x = 4.5.
y-m-36-10.s.s1.explain: Since w = 20 − 2x, the area is x(20 − 2x). x(20 − 2x) ≥ 48 becomes x² − 10x + 24 ≤ 0, that is, (x − 4)(x − 6) ≤ 0, so 4 ≤ x ≤ 6. Here w = 20 − 2x is at most 12 and at least 8, so it is always positive.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.prompt: The real wall is 10 m long, so w ≤ 10 must hold. Enter two (x, w) with different x that have an area of at least 48 ㎡ and use all 20 m of the rope. (x may be a decimal in steps of 0.5)
y-m-36-10.s.s2.hint.0: Turn w ≤ 10 into an inequality in x and overlap it with the interval you got in the previous step.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.hint.1: Pick two values of x in the overlapping interval, and calculate w and the area to check.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.fail.c1: x and w must be greater than 0.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.ok.c2: All 20 m of the rope is used.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.fail.c2: w + 2x is not 20. Check the condition that the whole rope is used.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.fail.c3: The area is less than 48 ㎡. Multiply x and w.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.ok.c4: The wall length is 10 m or less.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.fail.c4: w exceeds the wall length of 10 m.
y-m-36-10.s.s2.explain: From w ≤ 10, 20 − 2x ≤ 10, so x ≥ 5, and from the area condition x ≤ 6, so 5 ≤ x ≤ 6. (5, 10) has area 50, (5.5, 9) has 49.5, and (6, 8) has 48. (4, 12) has area 48, but the length 12 m exceeds the wall length 10 m, so it is not allowed. (7, 6) has area 42, which falls short.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.prompt: If the wall is only 8 m long (w ≤ 8), is a garden with an area of at least 48 ㎡ possible?
y-m-36-10.s.s3.hint.0: Turn w ≤ 8 into an inequality in x and overlap it with the earlier interval 4 ≤ x ≤ 6.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the overlapping part is an interval or a point.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.o.a: Impossible. The wall is short, so the area does not reach 48.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.r.a: This judgment says that once a limit appears, the goal cannot be reached. Find w and the area at the boundary value x = 6.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.o.b: Every value of x that is 6 or more is possible.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.r.b: You reflected only the wall limit and left out the area condition x ≤ 6. Find the area when x = 7.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.o.c: Every value of x from 4 to 6 is possible.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.r.c: You did not reflect the wall limit. See what w is when x = 4.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.r.d: You checked the case where the intervals of the two conditions meet at only one point.
y-m-36-10.s.s3.explain: From w ≤ 8, 20 − 2x ≤ 8, so x ≥ 6, and from the area condition x ≤ 6, so only x = 6 is left. Here w = 8 and the area is 48 ㎡, so the two conditions just touch exactly.
